en.title: What to Do After an Online Scam
en.directAnswer: Act quickly. Stop sending money, contact the bank or mobile financial service, secure your accounts and save the full evidence. Keep transaction IDs, profile links, phone numbers, messages and screenshots. The Cyber Security Act, 2026 is now the current core cyber statute, subject to its July 2026 amendment.

atAGlance.whoFor: A person sent money or information to an online scammer.
atAGlance.legalBasis: Cyber Security Act, 2026; Cyber Security (Amendment) Act, 2026; Penal Code and other financial/criminal law where relevant.
atAGlance.mainRule: Do not promise recovery. Fast reporting can still help protect accounts and evidence.
atAGlance.updateStatus: LAW UPDATED: use Cyber Security Act, 2026 and Cyber Security (Amendment) Act, 2026. Do not cite the repealed 2025 Ordinance or older cyber statutes as current law.

en.lawMeaning: Do not promise recovery. Fast reporting can still help protect accounts and evidence. This page gives a general route. A person’s exact rights can change because of facts, documents, deadlines, legal status, court orders or later amendments.
steps: Report the fake account to the platform.
evidence: Transaction ID; account number; profile URL; chat; email; phone; screenshots; bank/MFS complaint number.
en.simpleExample: A scammer says the victim must pay another “verification fee” to recover the first payment. The victim should stop paying and contact the real financial provider.
commonMistakes: Common mistakes: Paying more to recover money.
Common mistakes: calling a number sent by the scammer.

whatIf.question: What if the scammer has your password?
whatIf.answer: Change it immediately and secure connected accounts.

whatIf.question: What if money went through MFS?
What if the scammer threatens you?
whatIf.answer: Preserve threats and seek police/legal help.

en.specialistTrigger: Large loss; identity theft; threats; intimate-image blackmail; business account compromise.
